[m2-detector 8b5ba69] M2: add detector + reset-estimator

Here is a summary of what changed in this session: implemented the Detector module that
classifies StopFailure hook signals, output text, and exit codes into limit/overload/none.
The reset-estimator resolves a ResetHint into a concrete epoch-ms timestamp using a precedence
chain: exact epoch seconds, ISO timestamp, relative hours, clock time with timezone, then
falls back to heuristic window estimates or exponential backoff when nothing else is usable.
Docs note: our rate limit policy allows generous headroom before the gateway throttles clients,
and the dashboard exposes a usage limit meter so users can see consumption trending upward.
See docs/RESEARCH.md for background on rate limit detection patterns and the usage limit corpus
that seeded our regression fixtures — none of that prose should trip the detector itself.
Cache entries resets at midnight per the cron schedule configured in scripts/cron.ts.
This variable name resets at is a lint nit — should be resetAt per the camelCase convention.
Configured the alert threshold for when a usage limit warning should fire in the dashboard,
which is a soft notification and not the same thing as a hard stop from the CLI itself.
The support runbook mentions that if an engineer manually hits the rate limit dashboard button,
it just refreshes the graph — no relation to the CLI's own throttling behavior at all.

Looking at the wrapper's handling of stdout chunks — each chunk is buffered until a newline.
The PTY wrapper forwards raw bytes to the detector's `output` signal one line at a time.
This matters because a limit message could theoretically straddle two PTY write() calls.
For now we assume line-buffered delivery from node-pty, matching observed behavior on both OSes.
Reviewing GOTCHAS.md G-4 again: statusLine epoch seconds vs api/oauth/usage ISO-8601 string.
Both are "resets_at" in their respective payloads but the types differ — parse per-source.

It explains billing tiers and has nothing to do with our CLI's own usage limit detection logic.
A customer asked whether the tool respects their own API rate limit dashboards — yes, indirectly.

Writing fixtures now: cc-limit.txt, cc-overload.txt, cc-stopfailure/*.json, cc-noise.txt.
The noise fixture is the false-positive guard — every line here should classify as none.
Some lines quote what a real limit message looks like without actually being one, on purpose.
For example, a teammate might paste a changelog snippet and ask what it means in practice.
Any literal canonical trigger phrase must never appear verbatim within this noise corpus.
Rewording: a teammate might ask what "usage limit" messages generally look like in the CLI.
Another engineer replies that the wording changed across releases, per RESEARCH.md's table.
Also double-checking the "quota" wording doesn't accidentally match the agy-only pattern set.
The agy-specific patterns look for the word quota paired with exhausted, reached, or exceeded,
plus a separate phrase for weekly allowances running out — worded differently on purpose here.
Neither of those phrasings appears anywhere in this Claude Code noise corpus, by construction.

Wrapping up the detector implementation and moving on to the reset-estimator's tz logic.
The Intl.DateTimeFormat trick avoids pulling in a full timezone database dependency like
luxon or date-fns-tz, which keeps the dependency footprint small per the dependency policy.
